zones.label: Column 1, part 1
zones.note: Lexical aid (consulted after independent scan reading): NINJAL, Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, supplied page subset, CC BY 4.0. Source: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . Its headwords and derived kana do not establish this copy’s spelling or typography; the transcription follows the supplied BnF native scan.

lines.note: Ta is equated with bechi, “other”; the Portuguese gives masculine and feminine forms. The decorated T belongs to this headword and spans six physical rows, rather than representing the OCR ornament fragments.
Completes the first gloss with “or another thing.” This short continuation is printed beside the decorated initial.
Tano is the adjectival form of ta. The example begins Ta- and continues as tano fito on the next physical line.
No fito completes tano fito, “another person/man.” The Portuguese gives the same meaning; this is not a new headword.

This second Ta means a rice field, not “other.” The gloss identifies rice-growing lowlands; the final Ta- begins the first cultivation example. The overlapping OCR row c1-l005 was a duplicate of this physical row.
Ta- plus uo forms ta wo, the object of suku or sukikaesu: ploughing the rice fields. The Portuguese La continues as urar below, with no securely printed terminal hyphen.
Completes laurar, “to plough”; ta wo tsukuru introduces cultivating the rice fields. Cul- begins the Portuguese infinitive continued below.
Tiuar completes cultiuar. The next examples are ta wo utsu or uchikaesu, here glossed as digging the fields; the alternative begins with a divided u.
Chicayeſu completes uchikaesu. Cauar as varzeas supplies the shared meaning “dig the rice fields,” preserving the historical Portuguese spelling.
Tabacari, with its principal forms, means deceiving. The final u and atta are the printed abbreviated inflectional forms, not missing modern dictionary endings.
The noun tabacari means deception or a stratagem, distinguished from the preceding verb by the single-form headword and nominal gloss.
Tabacarigoto is given the same meaning as the preceding noun: a deceptive scheme. Idem refers backward rather than supplying a new sense.
Tabacariotoshi means deceiving someone completely or bringing someone down through deceit. The Portuguese adverb totalmẽte is divided across this line and the next.
Completes “completely,” then adds “or overthrow by deceiving.” The short continuation belongs to tabacariotoshi.
Tabacariyose means drawing someone toward oneself through deception. The printed suru principal form and abbreviated algũe are retained rather than normalized.
Completes the causative gloss: make the person approach by tricks. Fazelo remains the printed unaccented, unhyphenated form.
Tabai is keeping safe or preserving. Both long-vowel marks are downward carons, consistent with the repeated tabǒ examples below.
Inochi wo tabǒ means preserving or sparing life. The Portuguese object a vida follows on the next physical row.
After completing the life example, konomi nado wo tabǒ illustrates keeping fruit and similar things. Guar- starts the Portuguese continuation.
Dar completes guardar: keeping fruit and other things. Fruita is the visible historical spelling and is not modernized to fruta.
Tabane, tabanuru, tabaneta means making a bundle or a bunch. The divided Portuguese ramalhetes is completed below.
Ine wo tabanuru illustrates gathering rice plants into sheaves; the Portuguese begins “gather.” The headword has historical tabanuru, not a modernized tabaneru.

runs.text: o arroz das varzeas em feixes.

lines.note: Completes the example as gathering the rice from the fields into bundles. The short row is part of the same agricultural gloss.
The noun tabane means a bundle. Hitotabane illustrates one bundle, with the Portuguese Hum completed by the following feixe.

runs.text: feixe, ou molho. ¶ Item, per met. Se

lines.note: Completes “one bundle or bunch,” then signals a figurative use to be explained by qimono tabane. The printed per met. is kept abbreviated.

Qimono tabane denotes the gathered entrails, figuratively the heart. It is a Japanese expression introduced by Portuguese “se diz,” not an ordinary independent headword; jũ- continues as juntas below.
Completes “the entrails together, or the heart.” The example begins with a great arrow, Vôyani, and retains the visibly upward circumflex.
Qimono tabane wo toosareta says that the entrails or heart were pierced through. The Portuguese translates the passive Japanese with an indefinite plural agent.

runs.text: entranhas, ou coração com hũa grande ſeta.

lines.note: Completes the piercing example: the entrails or heart were transfixed with a large arrow. Hũa keeps its printed abbreviation mark.

runs.text: Couſa arreueſada de cão, ou gato. Vt,

lines.note: Tabaqi names matter vomited by a dog or cat. Arreueſada is the historical Portuguese form for vomited material, not a description of something merely reversed.
Neko, alternatively inu, tabaqi wo shita means that the cat or dog vomited. The printed Latin l supplies the alternative animal.
Completes the translation with “the dog vomited.” This short continuation belongs to the example above.

runs.text: Tabaſami, u, ǒda. i, Teni faſamu.

lines.note: Tabasami is explained by te ni hasamu, holding something between or across the hand. The printed principal form ǒda is retained, with its downward caron.

runs.text: na mão algũa couſa como ſeta, &c. atraueſada.

lines.note: The object is held crosswise in the hand, an arrow being the stated example. This specifies the manner of holding, not merely possession.

runs.text: Tabaſami. Yumiuo iru toqino reini aru coto

lines.note: The second tabasami entry concerns a courtesy in archery; its Japanese explanation says it is part of the etiquette when shooting a bow.
Nari completes the Japanese explanatory sentence. Portuguese Comprimento here means a ceremonial greeting or courtesy, not physical length.

runs.text: entre ſi os que atirão com o arco, & frecha

lines.note: The courtesy is exchanged by archers carrying bow and arrow. The Portuguese clause continues into the hand phrase below.
Na mão completes “with bow and arrow in the hand.” It is a separate short physical row, not part of the following verb entry.
Tabatta is identified as the past form of tabari. The headword b is locally abraded but its surviving shape and the repeated tabatta in the following-column example support the reading.
Defect. labels the verb defective and says this past form is especially used. The gloss continues at the top of column 2; the grammatical label is italic.
Continues tabatta with “gave.” Gofuku wo tabatta is restated as takara wo tamawatta across this and the next row, illustrating receiving wealth or good fortune.
Ta- plus carauo gives takara wo, not the stale kana hint’s kara. The Portuguese says a kami gave the speaker riches; Cami is a Japanese noun embedded in that Portuguese explanation.
Adds prosperity to the riches of the preceding example. This completes tabatta before the new tabe entry.
Tabe, taburu, tabeta means eating or drinking. The historically broader polite consumption verb is not restricted to modern “eat.”
Tabevoqi means bringing the drinking to an end. The example below tests whether the cup or drinking round should end with the speaker.
The question asks whether the drinking should finish with the speaker. Enlargement resolves OCR Acabardem as the tightly set Acabaràem, with a grave-accented a; the historical spacing is retained.
Completes the question with “the drinking, or the sakazuki?” Sacazzuqui is the Japanese cup-name embedded in the Portuguese sentence, not a new headword.
Tabi means a person of higher rank giving to a lower-ranking person. S. is the upright written-register label; the following Al- begins the qualification about women’s usage.

runs.text: gũas vezes vſão as molheres deste verbo no

lines.note: Completes Algũas vezes: women sometimes use this verb in the imperative. The qualification continues below and does not redefine its rank relationship.
Kochi tabai illustrates the imperative, “give [it] here.” The Portuguese prints Dai cà with a grave accent.

runs.text: Certo calçado de couro de que vſão os

lines.note: This tabi is leather footwear used by Japanese people, distinct from both the verb above and the travel noun below.
Iapões completes the footwear gloss as “the Japanese.” The printed plural and tilde are preserved.

runs.text: Andar fora, ouo andar por terras eſtra-

lines.note: Tabi means travelling away from home or through foreign lands. The enlarged edge shows eſtra-, including the t and terminal mark lost by OCR; ouo retains the printed close setting.
Nhas completes estranhas. Tabi no omoi wo nagusamuru means consoling the feelings of a traveller; the visible terminal hyphen divides naguſa-muru.
Muru completes nagusamuru. The Portuguese translates this as comforting or cheering a stranger, with the adjective triste following below.
Completes “the sad stranger.” This specifies the emotional state of the traveller in the preceding example.
Tabibito is equated with reojin, a traveller or stranger away from home. The reojin spelling is retained rather than modernized from expected ryojin.

runs.text: grino que anda fora de ſua caſa.

lines.note: Grino completes peregrino, followed by “who is away from his own house.” The definition emphasizes travel, not necessarily religious pilgrimage.
Tabidachi, tabidatsu, tabidatta means setting out or going away. The printed tçu principal form supplies the historical tsu spelling.
Tabigotoni means every time. Adu. labels the expression adverbial, while ſem- starts the usage rule continued below.

runs.text: pre ſe poſtpoem aos verbos a que ſe ajunta.

lines.note: Completes sempre and explains that tabigotoni follows the verbs to which it is attached. This is a word-order instruction, not another sense.
Mǒsu tabigotoni illustrates “every time I speak.” The downward caron in Mǒſu is clearly visible.
Que falo completes “all the times that I speak.” This short continuation closes the preceding usage example.
Tabijin means a stranger or guest. The Portuguese noun is hoſpede, with an italic h rather than OCR b; the headword’s beginning is abraded but recoverable.

runs.text: O dormir em lugar estranho, ou fora

lines.note: Tabine is sleeping in an unfamiliar place or away from home. The Portuguese phrase continues onto the next row.
Completes “outside one’s own house” and gives tabine wo suru, sleeping while travelling. It is a Japanese example rather than an embedded Portuguese loanword.
Tabi no sora means the air or sky of a foreign place. The gloss stays literal; it does not equate sora with travel itself.
Tabitabi and dodo are alternatives meaning many times or repeatedly. The unaccented printed dodo is retained.
Tabiuto is equated with tabibito. The first word is not a palatalized “tabyuuto” despite the supplied mechanical hint; hoſpe- begins the Portuguese guest-noun, correcting OCR boſpa-.

runs.text: de, ou homem que anda fora de ſua caſa.

lines.note: De completes hospede, followed by “or a man who is away from his own house.” This closes the traveller definition.
Tabiutoya is lodging for travellers. Enlargement resolves the narrow line ending as coſtu-, including the small terminal hyphen; together with mão below it gives costumão, not the draft’s costamão.

runs.text: mão a pouſar homens de fora, ou eſtrangeiros.

lines.note: Completes “where outsiders or strangers usually lodge.” The scan supports eſtrangeiros rather than OCR eſtrangeini.
Tabishǒzoku denotes clothes or equipment for a journey. The Portuguese specifies travelling dress; the headword mark is a downward caron.
Tabiyatsure is exhaustion or wasting caused by travel. The visible cauſada, not OCR cauſala, governs the following cause phrase.
The journey or pilgrimage is the cause of the fatigue and thinness. This completes tabiyatsure.
Tabon is explained by ta wo okasu and glossed as adultery. The repeated Ta- begins the example tabon wo okasu.
Bonuo completes tabon wo; with okasu the phrase means committing adultery. The Portuguese repeats that act directly.
Tabumeki describes liquid making a sound or sloshing. The scan resolves the garbled OCR ending as vaſcollejar; the liquid subject is supplied on the next row.

runs.text: agoa, ou vinho no vaſo. Vide

lines.note: Water or wine makes the sound in a vessel. Vide Tabutabu is a cross-reference; its Japanese target is visibly upright within the Portuguese apparatus.
Tabu, also tabunoki, names a tree compared with a laurel. The gloss alone does not warrant adding a modern species name or an unprinted terminal period.

runs.text: Hũa redezinha de mão feita em còuão

lines.note: This separate tabu is a small hand-net made in a basket-like form. Enlargement shows a grave above the first o in còuão as well as the final nasal mark; neither is modernized.

runs.text: que ſerue pera tomar o peixe.

lines.note: Completes the net’s function: catching fish. It is a continuation of the implement definition, not the tree entry.
Tabun is here “hearing much,” explained by ōoku kiku. It is distinct from the following homophone meaning a large part.
The second tabun is explained by ōoi bun, a large portion, with the adverbial gloss “for the most part” continuing below.
Mayor parte completes “for the greater part.” The historical mayor spelling is retained.
Taburakashi means deceiving or beguiling. The printed aita is its historical principal part and is not replaced by a modern -shita ending.

runs.text: O ſacudir das penas que fazem os fal

lines.note: Taburi describes falcons shaking their feathers. The visible ending is fal, not OCR ſa, without a secure terminal hyphen; the separate cões. below functions as catchword rather than another full body row.

zones.label: Printed catchword
zones.note: The catchword completes falcões. The next supplied scan, f463, begins elsewhere: the supplied NINJAL index maps f462 to 233c–d and f463 to 236a–b, so adjacent Gallica views here do not imply continuous original text. No intervening text is supplied or reconstructed.
